title: Who Else But Us
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Responding to teachers who complain that learning isn't valued in students' homes, Stuart makes two arguments. First, he cautions against assuming teachers can accurately judge what is or isn't valued inside a student's home, noting that families are complex and that even his own children's behavior wouldn't reliably reveal his family's values to an outside observer. Second, he argues that even when a student's home genuinely is hostile to the value of school, the teacher remains the person most responsible and best positioned to cultivate Value for that specific subject during the time the student is in their class. He frames this as empowering rather than blaming: it isn't a teacher's fault if a student never comes to value learning, but it is a failure of effort if the teacher doesn't relentlessly try. The piece closes by extending the argument across disciplines, insisting every teacher is uniquely responsible for selling the goodness of their own subject.
points: Stuart challenges the common teacher assumption that a student's home life can be read accurately from classroom behavior, calling for epistemic humility about families.
He separates outcome-responsibility from effort-responsibility: teachers aren't at fault if a student never values learning, but they are at fault if they don't relentlessly try to cultivate it.
The argument that no one else in the student's life is more responsible or capable is applied across disciplines, art, PE, math, not just Stuart's own subject.
The piece reframes a common source of teacher frustration, blaming unsupportive homes, into a call to control what is actually controllable: the classroom itself.
quotes: It's profoundly misguided for me to assume that I can make claims about what is and isn't valued in a student's home. I've been doing this long enough to have many, many students and families surprise me by revealing things, months or years into knowing them.
Basically, folks are complex; homes and families, even more so. We're better off with a humbler, "I know less than I think" kind of stance toward our students' homes.

There is no one else in the lives of my students more responsible for cultivating Value for learning in my subject area, during the year that my students are with me, than I am. No one is more responsible. No one is better equipped.
This doesn't mean it's our fault if students don't come to value learning while they're with us. It just means that it's our fault if we don't relentlessly aim to bring this increase in Value about.

But regardless of what happens at home, the good news is that the realm I control is powerful. In my classroom — and in yours — there can be grown the kind of life-giving counter-culture where learning is good because it's good.
